Mauritius.fact: The dodo, the most famous extinct bird in history, was endemic to the island and was driven to extinction by the 1680s, barely 80 years after humans arrived.
The 'Underwater Waterfall' illusion off the coast of Le Morne is created by sand and silt on the ocean floor flowing off an underwater plateau, visible from the air.
The island has one of the highest population densities in Africa and has transformed from a sugar-dependent economy to a diversified one including textiles, tourism, and financial services.
The Seven Coloured Earths of Chamarel are sand dunes with naturally occurring layers of seven distinct colours that never erode into a single shade despite rainfall.

Mexico.fact: The Chicxulub crater on the Yucatán Peninsula is the impact site of the asteroid that caused the mass extinction of dinosaurs 66 million years ago.
The country is home to the world's smallest volcano — Cuexcomate in Puebla is just 13 metres tall with a staircase leading into its crater.
Monarch butterflies migrate up to 4,500 km from Canada and the US to winter in the oyamel fir forests of Michoacán — an estimated billion butterflies arrive each year.
The ancient city of Teotihuacán, with its Pyramid of the Sun, once had a population of over 100,000 and was one of the largest cities in the world around 400 AD.
The country has 35 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, more than any other country in the Americas.
The name for "Chihuahua" dogs comes from the Mexican state, but the Aztecs believed they were sacred guides for the souls of the dead.

Micronesia.fact: Yap Island still uses rai stones — large circular limestone discs up to 4 metres in diameter — as a form of traditional currency, even though some weigh several tonnes.
Nan Madol, a ruined city of stone palaces built on 92 artificial islands in a lagoon, is sometimes called the 'Venice of the Pacific' and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Chuuk (Truk) Lagoon contains the wrecks of over 60 Japanese warships and aircraft sunk during a 1944 US air raid, making it one of the world's premier wreck-diving destinations.

Moldova.fact: The Mileștii Mici wine cellar holds the Guinness World Record for the largest wine collection — over 2 million bottles stored in 200 km of underground tunnels.
Transnistria, a narrow strip of land along the Ukrainian border, has its own government, currency, and military but is not recognised by any UN member state.
Despite being one of Europe's poorest countries, its wine industry is a major economic driver, with vineyards covering about 3.8% of the national territory.
The country has one of the highest rates of emigration in Europe — roughly a quarter of the population lives abroad.
It is home to the Mileștii Mici winery, which holds the Guinness World Record for the largest wine cellar by number of bottles (over 2 million).

Monaco.fact: At just 2.02 square kilometres, it is the second-smallest country in the world, yet has the highest population density of any sovereign nation at over 19,000 people per square kilometre.
About one in three residents is a millionaire, giving it the highest concentration of wealth per capita in the world.
The Monte Carlo Casino, opened in 1863, was built specifically to save the royal family from bankruptcy, and citizens of Monaco are forbidden from gambling there.
The Monaco Grand Prix is run through the streets of the principality and is considered one of the most prestigious motor races in the world, held annually since 1929.
It is so small that the entire country could fit into New York City's Central Park—and you'd still have room left over.

Mongolia.fact: It is the most sparsely populated sovereign country in the world, with roughly 2 people per square kilometre — about 30% of the population still lives as nomadic herders.
The Genghis Khan equestrian statue near Ulaanbaatar stands 40 metres tall and is the largest equestrian statue in the world.
The Mongolian Empire under Genghis Khan and his successors was the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe at its peak.
The Gobi Desert contains some of the world's most important dinosaur fossil sites — the first confirmed dinosaur eggs were discovered here in 1923.
There are more horses in Mongolia than there are people; the ratio is roughly 13 to 1.

Montenegro.fact: The Bay of Kotor, a winding fjord-like inlet, is often called the southernmost fjord in Europe, though it is technically a submerged river canyon.
Tara River Canyon, at 1,300 metres deep, is the deepest river canyon in Europe and the second-deepest in the world after the Grand Canyon.
Our Lady of the Rocks is a tiny artificial island in the Bay of Kotor, created over centuries by locals dropping stones and sinking old ships.
The country's name literally means 'Black Mountain', referring to the dark appearance of Mount Lovćen when covered in dense forest.

Montserrat.fact: The Soufrière Hills volcano erupted in 1995, burying the capital Plymouth under metres of ash and rock — it remains the only ghost town serving as an official capital.
Roughly two-thirds of the island is an exclusion zone, and the pre-eruption population of 11,000 dropped to under 5,000.
The island was known as the 'Emerald Isle of the Caribbean' due to its Irish heritage — St Patrick's Day is a public holiday commemorating both Irish settlers and a 1768 slave uprising.

Morocco.fact: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859 AD, is recognised by UNESCO and Guinness World Records as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
The Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca has the tallest minaret in the world at 210 metres and is one of the few mosques open to non-Muslims.
The Todra Gorge features 300-metre limestone canyon walls narrowing to just 10 metres apart, creating one of the most dramatic geological formations in North Africa.
Argan trees are found almost exclusively here, and goats famously climb them to eat the fruit — argan oil has become one of the world's most expensive culinary and cosmetic oils.

Mozambique.fact: The country's flag is the only one in the world to feature a modern assault rifle — an AK-47 crossed with a hoe, symbolising defence and agriculture.
The Bazaruto Archipelago is home to one of the last viable populations of dugongs in the western Indian Ocean.
Mozambique Island (Ilha de Moçambique) was a major Portuguese trading post and the original capital — the entire country is named after it.
Lake Malawi's southeastern shore falls within the country, where it is known as Lake Niassa.
It is the only country with a modern weapon (an AK-47) featured on its national flag.

Myanmar.fact: Bagan contains over 2,000 surviving Buddhist temples and pagodas built between the 9th and 13th centuries, spread across a 104-square-kilometre plain.
The country is one of only three (with Liberia and the US) that has not officially adopted the metric system.
Inle Lake's leg-rowing fishermen wrap one leg around their oar while balancing on the stern with the other, a technique unique to this lake.
The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is covered in hundreds of gold plates and topped with 5,448 diamonds and 2,317 rubies.
People here often wear a yellowish-white cosmetic paste called Thanaka, made from ground bark, which serves as both sunscreen and a beauty treatment.

Namibia.fact: The Namib Desert is considered the oldest desert in the world, having been arid for roughly 55-80 million years.
Kolmanskop, a former diamond-mining town, was abandoned in 1954 and is now half-buried in sand, creating one of the most photogenic ghost towns on Earth.
The Skeleton Coast is littered with the remains of shipwrecks and whale bones, and the Bushmen called it 'The Land God Made in Anger'.
It was the first African country to incorporate environmental protection into its constitution, and roughly 44% of the land is under conservation management.
Features a unique stretch where the desert dunes meet the sea directly.

Nauru.fact: At just 21 square kilometres, it is the world's smallest island nation and the third-smallest country by area.
Phosphate mining once made it the richest country per capita on Earth in the late 1960s, but reserves were exhausted, leaving 80% of the island a barren moonscape.
It is the only country in the world without an official capital city — government offices are located in the Yaren district.

Nepal.fact: The country contains eight of the world's fourteen peaks over 8,000 metres, including Mount Everest at 8,849 metres.
Lumbini, the birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) around 563 BC, is one of the holiest sites in Buddhism.
The Kumari tradition selects a young girl to be worshipped as the living incarnation of the goddess Taleju until she reaches puberty.
The country's calendar runs 56 years and 8 months ahead of the Gregorian calendar — Bikram Sambat is the official calendar.

Netherlands.fact: About a third of the country lies below sea level, and without its system of dykes, levees, and pumps, 65% of the land would be underwater at high tide.
During the 17th-century 'Tulip Mania', single tulip bulbs sold for more than 10 times a skilled craftsman's annual salary — one of history's first recorded speculative bubbles.
There are more bicycles than people — roughly 23 million bikes for 17.5 million inhabitants — and the country has over 35,000 km of dedicated cycle paths.
The world's first stock exchange was established in Amsterdam in 1602 to trade shares of the Dutch East India Company.
There are more bicycles than people in the Netherlands, and the country has specialized "bicycle traffic jams."

New Caledonia.fact: The territory has the world's largest enclosed lagoon, covering 24,000 square kilometres and surrounded by the world's second-longest double barrier reef.
It holds roughly 25% of the world's known nickel reserves, making mining the economic backbone of the territory.
The kagu, a flightless bird found only here, has no close living relatives and is the sole surviving member of its entire family (Rhynochetidae).

New Zealand.fact: The country was the last major landmass to be settled by humans — Polynesians arrived only around 1250-1300 AD.
In 1893, it became the first self-governing country in the world to grant all women the right to vote in national elections.
The kiwi bird has nostrils at the tip of its beak (unique among birds) and lays an egg that is up to 25% of the mother's body weight — the largest egg-to-body ratio of any bird.
Milford Sound receives roughly 8 metres of rain per year, creating temporary waterfalls that cascade down cliffs during storms.
It was the first country to give women the right to vote in 1893.

Nicaragua.fact: Lake Nicaragua (Lake Cocibolca) contains the world's only freshwater sharks — bull sharks that have adapted to swim up the San Juan River from the Caribbean.
The country has the only flag in the world (besides El Salvador's) that features the colour purple, visible in the rainbow on its coat of arms.
Cerro Negro, one of the youngest volcanoes in Central America (born in 1850), is popular for 'volcano boarding' — sliding down its ash-covered slopes at speeds up to 95 km/h.
It is the largest country in Central America by area, yet one of the least densely populated.

Niger.fact: The Sahara Desert covers about 80% of the country's territory, yet the area around the Niger River in the southwest supports most of the population.
The Cure Salée ('Salt Cure') festival sees Tuareg and Wodaabe nomads converge annually for camel races and the Gerewol, a male beauty contest where men dance elaborately to attract wives.
The Tree of Ténéré was considered the most isolated tree on Earth — the only one for over 400 km in any direction — until a truck driver knocked it down in 1973.
Agadez contains one of the oldest mud-brick minarets in West Africa, the Grand Mosque, which has been standing since the 16th century.

Nigeria.fact: Nollywood produces more films per year than Hollywood, making it the second or third largest film industry in the world by volume.
The country has over 250 ethnic groups speaking over 500 distinct languages — more linguistic diversity than nearly any other African nation.
The Benin Bronzes, intricate metal plaques and sculptures from the Kingdom of Benin dating to the 13th century, are among the most famous examples of African art.
With over 220 million people, it is the most populous country in Africa and the seventh most populous in the world.
The city of Lagos is so large and fast-growing that it is projected to become the most populous city in the world by 2100.

Niue.fact: With a population of roughly 1,600, it is one of the smallest self-governing states in the world, yet it was the first country to offer free nationwide Wi-Fi.
The entire island is essentially a raised coral atoll, and there are no rivers or streams — all freshwater comes from underground.
The island issued legal tender coins featuring Disney characters and Pokémon, making them some of the most unusual currency in the world.

Norfolk Island.fact: The island was settled in 1856 by descendants of the Bounty mutineers who were relocated from overcrowded Pitcairn Island, and many residents still speak Norfuk, a creole of 18th-century English and Tahitian.
The towering Norfolk Island pine, now an ornamental tree found worldwide, is native only to this tiny island.
The island's convict settlement ruins from the 18th and 19th centuries are a UNESCO World Heritage Site documenting the harsh realities of British penal transportation.

North Korea.fact: The country uses its own calendar — the Juche calendar — which starts from the birth year of Kim Il-sung (1912), making 2026 the year Juche 115.
The Ryugyong Hotel in Pyongyang, a 330-metre pyramid-shaped skyscraper started in 1987, remains unfinished and unoccupied after nearly four decades of construction.
The DMZ (Demilitarised Zone) between North and South Korea has become an accidental nature reserve, with rare species like the red-crowned crane thriving in the undisturbed strip.
Pyongyang's metro system runs up to 110 metres underground, making it one of the deepest metro systems in the world, partly designed to serve as a nuclear bunker.
It has its own time zone (Pyongyang Time), which was created in 2015 by moving the clocks back 30 minutes to break away from "imperialist" Japanese time.

North Macedonia.fact: Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest and deepest lakes in Europe, dating back 2-3 million years, and contains numerous endemic species found nowhere else.
Mother Teresa was born in Skopje in 1910, though the city was then part of the Ottoman Empire.
The country changed its name from 'Macedonia' to 'North Macedonia' in 2019 to resolve a decades-long naming dispute with Greece.
The Stone Bridge over the Vardar River in Skopje dates to the 15th century and is the city's most recognisable symbol.

Northern Mariana Islands.fact: The Mariana Trench, the deepest point in the world's oceans at nearly 11,000 metres, lies just east of the islands.
Residents are US citizens but cannot vote in presidential elections, and the territory has a non-voting delegate in the US House of Representatives.
The island of Pagan has an active volcano that erupted in 1981, forcing the evacuation of all residents, and the island has remained largely uninhabited since.

Norway.fact: The country has a sovereign wealth fund worth over $1.5 trillion — roughly $280,000 for every citizen — built from oil and gas revenues.
Svalbard, in the Arctic, has a Global Seed Vault dug into a mountain that stores over one million seed samples from around the world as insurance against agricultural catastrophe.
The Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle experience the midnight sun for over two months, yet have surprisingly mild winters due to the Gulf Stream.
Slow TV originated here — a 7-hour train journey from Bergen to Oslo was broadcast in real time and watched by over 1.2 million viewers, about a quarter of the population.
The craggy explorer Thor Heyerdahl once waited hours for a taxi at the BBC because the driver was looking for "four Airedales".

Oman.fact: The Rub' al Khali (Empty Quarter) extends into the country's interior — it is the largest continuous sand desert in the world.
Frankincense has been harvested in the Dhofar region for over 5,000 years and was once worth more than gold — the trees are UNESCO-listed.
The Majlis al Jinn (Meeting Place of the Spirits) is one of the largest cave chambers in the world, so vast that several hot-air balloons have been flown inside it.
The Al Hajar Mountains contain some of the world's best-exposed sections of oceanic crust thrust onto land, making the country a pilgrimage site for geologists.

Pakistan.fact: K2, the second-tallest mountain in the world at 8,611 metres, has a fatality rate of roughly 1 in 4 climbers, making it far deadlier than Everest.
Mohenjo-daro, a 4,500-year-old Indus Valley city, had a sophisticated urban grid, indoor plumbing, and a public bath system centuries before the Roman Empire.
The Karakoram Highway, linking the country to China, is the highest paved international road in the world, reaching 4,693 metres at the Khunjerab Pass.
The country has more than 7,000 glaciers — more than anywhere outside the polar regions — and the Baltoro Glacier alone is 63 km long.
It is home to the world's highest ATM, located at the Khunjerab Pass at an elevation of 4,693 meters (15,397 feet).

Palau.fact: Jellyfish Lake contains millions of golden jellyfish that have evolved without stingers, allowing swimmers to safely float among them.
In 2009, it became the first country to create a shark sanctuary, banning all commercial shark fishing across its entire exclusive economic zone.
The Rock Islands, a collection of over 400 limestone islets covered in jungle, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site with some of the highest marine biodiversity in the world.

Palestine.fact: Jericho, in the West Bank, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, with evidence of settlement dating back over 10,000 years.
The Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, built over the traditional birthplace of Jesus, is one of the oldest continuously operating churches in the world.
Olive oil production is central to the culture and economy — some olive trees in the West Bank are estimated to be over 2,000 years old.
The city of Jericho is believed to be the oldest continuously inhabited city in the world, dating back over 10,000 years.

Panama.fact: The Panama Canal uses a system of locks that raises ships 26 metres above sea level to cross through Gatun Lake — roughly 14,000 vessels transit each year.
It is the only place in the world where you can watch the sun rise over the Pacific Ocean and set over the Atlantic, due to the country's S-shaped isthmus.
The country has more bird species than the United States and Canada combined — over 1,000 species in a territory smaller than South Carolina.
The Darién Gap, a 160-km stretch of dense jungle between Panama and Colombia, is the only break in the Pan-American Highway's 30,000-km route from Alaska to Patagonia.

Papua New Guinea.fact: The island of New Guinea has been inhabited for at least 50,000 years, making its indigenous peoples among the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.
The country's highland tribes were completely unknown to the outside world until the 1930s, when Australian gold prospectors stumbled upon a million people living in the interior.
Birds of paradise, with their extraordinary plumage displays, are found almost exclusively here and on nearby islands — there are 38 known species.
The country has no functioning national road network — most travel between major towns is by air, making it one of the most aviation-dependent countries in the world.

Paraguay.fact: It is one of only two landlocked countries in South America (the other is Bolivia) and contains the Gran Chaco, one of the last great wilderness areas on the continent.
The Itaipu Dam on the Paraguay-Brazil border is one of the most powerful hydroelectric plants in the world and supplies roughly 90% of Paraguay's electricity.
Guaraní is an official language alongside Spanish, and over 90% of the population speaks it — the only indigenous language in the Americas with such widespread use.
The Chaco War (1932–1935) with Bolivia was the deadliest South American conflict of the 20th century, fought over territory believed to hold oil reserves that were never found.

Peru.fact: Machu Picchu, the 15th-century Inca citadel perched 2,430 metres above sea level, was unknown to the outside world until Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911.
The Nazca Lines, enormous geoglyphs etched into the desert floor between 500 BC and 500 AD, include figures up to 370 metres long and can only be fully appreciated from the air.
The country has over 3,000 varieties of potato — more than any other country — as the potato was first domesticated in the Andes around 8,000 BC.
Cotahuasi Canyon, at over 3,354 metres deep, is one of the deepest canyons in the world — roughly twice the depth of the Grand Canyon.
Rainbow Mountain (Vinicunca), with its vivid stripes of red, gold, and turquoise caused by mineral deposits, was only revealed to tourists after its snow cap melted due to climate change.
This nation grows more than 2,800 varieties of potatoes, more than any other country on Earth.

Philippines.fact: The country consists of 7,641 islands, but only about 2,000 are inhabited, and many do not even have names.
The Chocolate Hills of Bohol — over 1,200 nearly identical conical hills — turn brown in the dry season, resembling a vast landscape of chocolate drops.
The Philippine Eagle, with a wingspan of over 2 metres, is one of the world's largest and most powerful raptors and is found nowhere else.
The Puerto Princesa Underground River flows 8.2 km through a cave system directly into the sea and is one of the longest navigable underground rivers in the world.

Poland.fact: The Wieliczka Salt Mine near Kraków has been operating since the 13th century and contains an entire underground cathedral, complete with chandeliers carved from rock salt.
Białowieża Forest, shared with Belarus, is the last remaining primeval forest in lowland Europe and is home to the European bison.
The country is the world's largest exporter of amber, and the Baltic coast regularly washes up pieces of the fossilised tree resin, some containing insects millions of years old.
Nicolaus Copernicus, who proposed the heliocentric model of the solar system in 1543, was born in Toruń — the discovery fundamentally changed humanity's understanding of the universe.

Portugal.fact: In 1755, Lisbon was struck by one of the deadliest earthquakes in European history, followed by a tsunami and fires that destroyed 85% of the city — it led to the birth of modern seismology.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge in Lisbon stretches 17.2 km, making it the longest bridge in Europe.

The Livraria Lello bookstore in Porto, with its dramatic neo-Gothic interior and crimson staircase, is often called one of the most beautiful bookstores in the world and reportedly inspired J.K. Rowling.
Cork production accounts for over 50% of the world's supply, harvested from the bark of cork oak trees every 9 years without harming the tree.
The song "Goodbye" by Paulo de Carvalho was used as the secret signal to start the Carnation Revolution in 1974

Puerto Rico.fact: Mosquito Bay on the island of Vieques is the brightest bioluminescent bay in the world, with microorganisms that flash blue-green when disturbed.
El Yunque is the only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest System and receives over 200 inches of rain per year.
The Arecibo Observatory housed the world's largest single-aperture radio telescope (305 metres) from 1963 until its collapse in 2020.
San Juan, founded in 1521, is the second-oldest European-established capital city in the Americas (after Santo Domingo).

Qatar.fact: The country will host the first FIFA World Cup in the Middle East in 2022 — and built seven entirely new stadiums, including one designed to be disassembled after the tournament.
The Pearl-Qatar, an artificial island, is a luxury development built on the former site of pearl diving beds that were the country's economic foundation before oil.
The peninsula has virtually no natural freshwater, so roughly 99% of the country's drinking water comes from desalinated seawater.
Al Jazeera, one of the most-watched news channels in the world, was founded in Doha in 1996 and broadcasts in multiple languages.
It is one of the few countries where the literacy rate is nearly 100%, and it has the highest GDP per capita in the world.

Romania.fact: The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is the heaviest building in the world and the largest civilian administrative building, with 1,100 rooms.
Bran Castle in Transylvania is marketed as 'Dracula's Castle', though Vlad the Impaler — the historical inspiration for Bram Stoker's character — likely only passed through.
The Danube Delta is Europe's largest wetland, home to over 300 species of birds and 45 freshwater fish species.
The Merry Cemetery in Săpânța features brightly painted wooden crosses with humorous poems describing the deceased's life — a unique and irreverent approach to death.

Russia.fact: The Trans-Siberian Railway stretches 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok, crossing 8 time zones — the longest railway line in the world.
Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world (1,642 m) and contains about 20% of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater.
The Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg has over 3 million items in its collection and employs a staff of cats to protect artworks from mice.
Oymyakon in Siberia recorded a temperature of −67.7°C in 1933, making it the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth.
It has a larger surface area than the entire planet of Pluto.

Rwanda.fact: Mountain gorillas in Volcanoes National Park have recovered from fewer than 250 individuals to over 1,000, one of the great conservation success stories.
The country banned single-use plastic bags in 2008, making it one of the first nations to do so — Kigali is now often called the cleanest city in Africa.
Women hold over 60% of seats in the national parliament, the highest proportion of any country in the world.
The country is known as the 'Land of a Thousand Hills' (Pays des Mille Collines) due to its undulating hilly terrain across nearly every part of the country.
This country has the highest percentage of women in parliament in the world, occupying over 60% of the seats.
Plastic bags are strictly illegal; they will be confiscated at the airport, and the country is now one of the cleanest in Africa.

Saint Barthelemy.fact: The island is the only Caribbean territory that was once a Swedish colony (1784–1878), and the capital Gustavia is named after King Gustav III of Sweden.
The airport runway ends just metres from the beach, where planes descend over a hilltop road — it is considered one of the most dramatic airport approaches in the world.
It is entirely duty-free, with no income tax, and has become one of the most exclusive luxury holiday destinations in the Caribbean.

Saint Helena.fact: Napoleon Bonaparte spent his final six years of exile on the island (1815–1821), and his former residence Longwood House is still maintained by the French government.
Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise living on the island, is the oldest known living land animal, born around 1832.
The island had no airport until 2017 — previously the only way to reach it was by ship, a five-day journey from Cape Town.

Saint Kitts and Nevis.fact: It is the smallest sovereign state in the Americas by both area and population — roughly 47,000 people across 261 square kilometres.
Brimstone Hill Fortress, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is one of the best-preserved historical fortifications in the Americas and was known as 'The Gibraltar of the West Indies'.
The Citizenship by Investment Programme, established in 1984, was the first of its kind in the world, allowing foreign nationals to obtain citizenship through investment.

Saint Lucia.fact: The Pitons — two volcanic spires rising over 700 metres from the sea — are the island's iconic UNESCO World Heritage landmark.
It is the only country in the world named after a woman — Saint Lucy of Syracuse.
The island has produced two Nobel Prize winners (Sir Arthur Lewis for Economics, Derek Walcott for Literature) — the highest per capita Nobel rate of any sovereign nation.

Saint Martin.fact: The island is the smallest landmass in the world divided between two sovereign states — France (north) and the Netherlands (south) — with an open border since 1648.
Maho Beach is famous for planes landing at Princess Juliana Airport directly overhead, with jet blast strong enough to knock people off their feet.
The French side has over 300 restaurants, earning it the nickname 'Gourmet Capital of the Caribbean'.

Saint Pierre and Miquelon.fact: It is the last remnant of France's once-vast North American empire (New France) and is only 25 km from the coast of Newfoundland.
During Prohibition in the United States (1920–1933), the islands became a major smuggling hub for Canadian whisky bound for the American market.
Despite being in North America, the territory uses the euro and has a distinctly French culture, with bakeries, cafés, and Basque-influenced architecture.

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.fact: La Soufrière volcano erupted in April 2021, forcing the evacuation of roughly 20,000 people — about a fifth of the population.
The Tobago Cays, a cluster of uninhabited islands with crystal-clear water, were used as a filming location for 'Pirates of the Caribbean'.
Breadfruit was first introduced to the Caribbean here by Captain Bligh of Bounty fame, on his second (successful) breadfruit voyage in 1793.

Samoa.fact: In 2011, the country skipped an entire day by switching from the east side to the west side of the International Date Line, jumping from Thursday 29 December directly to Saturday 31 December.
Robert Louis Stevenson spent the last four years of his life here and is buried atop Mount Vaea — the Samoans called him 'Tusitala' (Teller of Tales).
The traditional Samoan tatau (tattoo) covers the body from waist to knee and takes weeks to complete using hand-tapped instruments — the English word 'tattoo' derives from the Polynesian practice.

San Marino.fact: Founded in 301 AD, it claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic and one of the oldest continuously existing sovereign states.
The entire country is perched on and around Mount Titano, with three medieval fortresses on its peaks visible from miles around.
Despite a population of only about 33,000, the country has its own football team, Olympic committee, and more cars than people.
During World War II, it accepted over 100,000 refugees — more than 10 times its own population at the time.
It is the world’s oldest republic (founded in 301 AD) and, for a long time, had the world’s only postal system that used a "decimal" system for stamps.

Sao Tome and Principe.fact: The islands sit almost exactly on the Equator and the Prime Meridian, placing them near the geographic coordinates 0°N, 0°E.
Pico Cão Grande, a 370-metre volcanic plug rising from the jungle floor like a needle, is one of the most dramatic geological formations in Africa.
The islands were uninhabited when Portuguese explorers arrived in the 1470s and became a major centre of the sugar trade, later shifting to cocoa.

Saudi Arabia.fact: The Empty Quarter (Rub' al Khali) is the largest continuous sand desert in the world, covering an area roughly the size of France.
Mada'in Saleh (Hegra), the first UNESCO World Heritage Site in the country, contains 131 rock-cut tombs built by the Nabataean civilisation, similar to Petra in Jordan.
Women were only allowed to drive starting in June 2018, ending the world's last remaining ban on female drivers.
The NEOM megaproject includes 'The Line', a planned 170-km-long linear city with no cars and no streets, designed to house 9 million people.

The country imports sand and camels from Australia. Saudi sand is often too wind-blown for construction, and their native camels are mostly used for racing, while Australian camels are preferred for meat.

Senegal.fact: The Dakar Rally, one of the world's most famous off-road endurance races, originally ended in the capital Dakar (though the race moved to South America in 2009 and later Saudi Arabia).
Gorée Island, just offshore from Dakar, was a major departure point in the Atlantic slave trade and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The African Renaissance Monument in Dakar stands 49 metres tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty — and was controversially built by a North Korean construction company.
The country is known for its 'teranga' (hospitality) culture, and its national football team is nicknamed the Lions of Teranga.

Serbia.fact: Nikola Tesla, one of history's most important inventors (AC electricity, radio waves, the Tesla coil), was born in Smiljan, then part of the Austrian Empire, to Serbian parents.
The Đavolja Varoš ('Devil's Town') contains over 200 earth pyramids formed by erosion, some topped with stone caps, which local legend attributes to petrified wedding guests.
Belgrade, situated at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers, has been destroyed and rebuilt over 40 times throughout its history.
The country is one of the world's largest exporters of raspberries, producing roughly a third of the global supply.

Seychelles.fact: The Vallée de Mai on Praslin Island contains the endemic coco de mer palm, which produces the largest seed in the plant kingdom — up to 25 kg.
Aldabra Atoll is a UNESCO World Heritage Site home to the world's largest population of giant tortoises — over 100,000, outnumbering the Galápagos population.
With a population of roughly 100,000, it is the smallest African country by population and the least populous sovereign African nation.
The islands are made of granite rather than coral, making them the only mid-oceanic granite islands in the world.
It is the only country in the world made entirely of granite islands (most others are volcanic or coral).

Sierra Leone.fact: The name means 'Lion Mountains', given by Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra in 1462 because the shape of the mountains reminded him of a lion.
Freetown was founded in 1792 as a settlement for freed slaves from the American Revolution, making it one of the oldest established communities of free Black people in Africa.
The country has some of the world's most beautiful beaches, but Bunce Island in the Sierra Leone River was one of the largest British slave trading posts in West Africa.
The 'Star of Sierra Leone', discovered in 1972, was the third-largest gem-quality diamond ever found, weighing 968.9 carats.

Singapore.fact: The country has virtually no natural resources, yet has one of the highest GDPs per capita in the world, built on trade, finance, and manufacturing.
Chewing gum has been banned since 1992 (with exceptions for therapeutic gum), and littering, jaywalking, and failing to flush a public toilet are all finable offences.
The Changi Airport Jewel features the world's tallest indoor waterfall at 40 metres, surrounded by a terraced indoor forest.
Despite being a city-state of just 733 square kilometres, it has gained about 25% more land since independence through land reclamation.
A beauty contest held here in 1998 awarded 60% of its marks for the contestants' knowledge of the internet.

Sint Maarten.fact: The Dutch side of the shared island of Saint Martin is the smallest territory in the world that is part of two separate sovereign nations.
Great Bay Beach is famous for planes from Princess Juliana Airport passing just metres overhead on landing approach.
Despite its tiny size (34 square kilometres), it hosts over a million cruise ship passengers per year.

Slovakia.fact: The country has more castles and chateaux per capita than any other country in the world — over 180 for a population of 5.4 million.
The Dobšiná Ice Cave contains permanent ice formations up to 26 metres thick that have been there for thousands of years, despite the cave being at a relatively low altitude.
Andy Warhol's parents were from the village of Miková in northeastern Slovakia, and a museum dedicated to the pop art icon operates in nearby Medzilaborce.
Bratislava is the only national capital that borders two other sovereign countries — Austria and Hungary.

Slovenia.fact: Over 60% of the country is covered by forest, making it the third-most-forested country in Europe after Finland and Sweden.
Postojna Cave, 24 km of passages, has been a tourist attraction since 1819 and is home to the olm (proteus), a blind cave salamander that can live for over 100 years.
Lake Bled, with its island church and clifftop castle, was voted one of the most beautiful alpine lakes in Europe — the island is the only natural island in the country.
The Lipizzaner horses, famous for the Spanish Riding School in Vienna, originate from the village of Lipica in southwestern Slovenia.

Solomon Islands.fact: The islands were the site of fierce World War II battles, including Guadalcanal — wrecks of ships and aircraft still litter the surrounding waters, known as 'Iron Bottom Sound'.
Some islanders use dolphin teeth as traditional currency, and the practice of dolphin hunting and tooth trading continues on certain islands.
Kavachi, an active submarine volcano, is one of the most active in the Pacific and occasionally creates temporary islands that erode back below the surface.

Somalia.fact: The country has the longest coastline in mainland Africa, stretching over 3,000 km along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Laas Geel cave paintings near Hargeisa, dating back roughly 5,000 years, are among the best-preserved rock art in Africa, depicting cattle and human figures.
Frankincense and myrrh have been traded from the country since ancient times — the region was known as the 'Land of Punt' by ancient Egyptians.
Camel milk is a dietary staple, and the country has one of the largest camel populations in the world, estimated at over 7 million.

South Africa.fact: Table Mountain in Cape Town is estimated to be one of the oldest mountains in the world, around 600 million years old — six times older than the Himalayas.
The Cradle of Humankind, a UNESCO site near Johannesburg, has produced more hominid fossils than any other place on Earth, including 'Little Foot', a 3.67-million-year-old skeleton.
The Sardine Run along the KwaZulu-Natal coast is one of the largest marine migrations in the world, with billions of sardines attracting sharks, dolphins, and diving birds.
The first human-to-human heart transplant was performed by Dr Christiaan Barnard at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town in 1967.
It is the only country in the world to have three official capital cities: Pretoria (Executive), Bloemfontein (Judicial), and Cape Town (Legislative).

South Korea.fact: The DMZ between North and South Korea has accidentally become a wildlife corridor, hosting endangered species like the Asiatic black bear and red-crowned crane.
Jjimjilbangs (Korean bathhouses) are open 24 hours and function as social hubs where people eat, sleep, watch TV, and socialise — many Koreans use them as informal hotels.
The country went from one of the poorest in the world in the 1960s to having the 10th largest economy — a transformation known as the 'Miracle on the Han River'.
Hangul, the Korean alphabet created in 1443 by King Sejong the Great, was specifically designed to be easy to learn — it can be learned in a few hours.
It is considered bad luck or taboo to write a person's name in red ink.

South Sudan.fact: It is the youngest country in the world, having gained independence from Sudan on 9 July 2011 after a referendum in which 98.83% voted for separation.
The Sudd, one of the world's largest wetlands, is so vast that it absorbs over half of the White Nile's water flow, which is why the Nile loses enormous volume crossing the country.
The Mundari people of central South Sudan wash their cattle with the animals' own urine (which acts as an antiseptic) and sleep among their herds, coating themselves in ash for insect protection.
Oil accounts for roughly 98% of the government's revenue, making it one of the most oil-dependent economies in the world.

Spain.fact: La Tomatina festival in Buñol sees roughly 20,000 participants throw over 150 tonnes of tomatoes at each other in the world's largest food fight.
The Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882 and is expected to be completed around 2026 — over 140 years after work began.
The country has the second-highest number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the world, after Italy.
The Siesta tradition means many shops and businesses still close for 2–3 hours in the afternoon, and the country's prime-time TV starts at 10:30 PM.
Alhambra in Granada receives roughly 2.7 million visitors per year, making it the most-visited monument in Spain.
Traditionally, it is common to greet women with a kiss on each cheek, and the country is home to the famous annual Bull Run in Pamplona.

Sri Lanka.fact: The island has the highest biodiversity density in Asia — more species per square kilometre than any other country in the region.
Sigiriya is a 5th-century fortress built atop a 200-metre granite rock column, with elaborate gardens, frescoes, and a mirror wall.
The country is the world's fourth-largest tea producer, and 'Ceylon tea' (the island's former name) is still a globally recognised brand.
Adam's Peak (Sri Pada) features a boulder at its summit with a footprint-shaped impression claimed by Buddhists, Hindus, Christians, and Muslims as belonging to their respective religious figures.
The national anthem was originally written in Sanskrit and later translated into Sinhala and Tamil, but the two versions have slightly different melodies.

Sudan.fact: The ancient civilisation of Kush, centred in Nubia, had powerful queens (Kandakes) who ruled in their own right — Queen Amanirenas famously fought against Roman Emperor Augustus.
At the confluence of the Blue and White Nile in Khartoum, you can see the two rivers flowing side by side in different colours before merging.
Meroe was the capital of the Kingdom of Kush and contains over 200 pyramids — smaller and steeper than Egypt's, with many still largely intact.
Jebel Barkal, a flat-topped mountain near Karima, was considered sacred by both the ancient Egyptians and the Kushites, who built temples and pyramids at its base.

Suriname.fact: Over 90% of the country is covered by tropical rainforest, giving it one of the highest forest-coverage ratios of any nation on Earth.
It is the smallest country in South America by area and the only one with Dutch as its official language.
The country's population is remarkably diverse, including significant communities of Hindustani, Javanese, Maroon, Indigenous, Chinese, and European descent.
Central Suriname Nature Reserve covers 1.6 million hectares of pristine tropical forest and is home to the jaguar, giant armadillo, and harpy eagle.

Sweden.fact: The Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi is rebuilt entirely from ice and snow each winter and has been operating since 1989 — even the glasses at the bar are made of ice.
The country has a 'Right of Public Access' (Allemansrätten) that allows anyone to roam freely across private land, camp overnight, and pick berries and mushrooms.
ABBA's music generates more annual revenue than any other Swedish export category besides automobiles and iron.
The Vasa warship, which sank on its maiden voyage in 1628 after sailing just 1,300 metres, was raised from Stockholm harbour in 1961 and is now the most visited museum in Scandinavia.

Switzerland.fact: The country has not fought in a foreign war since 1515, making it one of the longest-standing neutral nations in the world.
There are enough nuclear bunkers to shelter the entire population — roughly 8.6 million spaces — more per capita than any other country.
CERN, on the Franco-Swiss border near Geneva, is where the World Wide Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016, is the world's longest and deepest traffic tunnel at 57.1 km, running up to 2,300 metres below the Alps.
It is illegal to own just one guinea pig because they are social animals and it is considered "animal cruelty" for them to be lonely.

Syria.fact: Damascus is widely considered the oldest continuously inhabited capital city in the world, with evidence of settlement dating back over 11,000 years.
The ancient city of Palmyra was a major trading centre on the Silk Road and contained some of the most spectacular Roman-era ruins in the Middle East.
Aleppo's Great Mosque contains what is claimed to be a relic of John the Baptist's father, Zechariah, and the city's souk (marketplace) was one of the longest covered markets in the world.
The Dead Cities, a group of about 700 abandoned settlements in northwestern Syria, provide the best-preserved examples of rural life in the late Roman and Byzantine periods.

Taiwan.fact: Taipei 101 was the world's tallest building from 2004 to 2010, and its 730-tonne tuned mass damper (visible to visitors) stabilises the tower against typhoons and earthquakes.
The island manufactures over 60% of the world's semiconductors and over 90% of the most advanced chips, making TSMC one of the most strategically important companies on Earth.
Taroko Gorge, carved through marble cliffs up to 1,000 metres deep, is one of the most dramatic natural formations in East Asia.
Night markets are a defining feature of the culture, with over 300 across the island serving everything from stinky tofu to bubble tea, which was invented here in the 1980s.
Garbage trucks here don’t just beep; they play classical music—usually Beethoven’s Für Elise—to let residents know it’s time to bring out their trash.

Tajikistan.fact: Over 93% of the country is mountainous, including the 7,495-metre Ismoil Somoni Peak, the highest point in the former Soviet Union.
The Fedchenko Glacier is the longest glacier outside the polar regions, stretching 77 km through the Pamir Mountains.
Lake Sarez was formed in 1911 when an earthquake created a massive natural dam — the lake is considered a major risk because a breach could flood millions of people downstream.
The Pamir Highway (M41) is one of the highest paved roads in the world, crossing passes above 4,600 metres.

Tanzania.fact: Mount Kilimanjaro is the tallest freestanding mountain in the world at 5,895 metres and the highest point in Africa, yet it sits just 3 degrees south of the equator.
The Serengeti wildebeest migration, involving over 1.5 million animals, is one of the largest mass movements of land mammals on Earth.
Tanzanite, a blue-violet gemstone found only in a 4-km strip near Mount Kilimanjaro, is 1,000 times rarer than diamonds.
Olduvai Gorge, in the Serengeti, has yielded some of the oldest known evidence of early human evolution, including 1.8-million-year-old Homo habilis remains.
Zanzibar's Stone Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was once the centre of the Indian Ocean spice trade and the Arab slave trade.

Thailand.fact: It is the only Southeast Asian country never to have been colonised by a European power, maintaining its independence while neighbours fell to Britain and France.
The full ceremonial name of Bangkok in Thai has 168 characters, making it the longest city name in the world.
The floating markets of Damnoen Saduak and Amphawa, where vendors sell goods from boats, have been a trading tradition for over two centuries.
The country is the world's largest exporter of rice and natural rubber, and Thai massage was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2019.
It is illegal to step on any currency (Baht) because it bears the image of the King, and doing so is considered an act of "lese-majeste."

Timor-Leste.fact: It became the first new sovereign state of the 21st century when it gained independence from Indonesia on 20 May 2002.
The Atauro Island reef has been recorded as having the highest concentration of reef fish species at a single site anywhere in the world.
The country's petroleum fund, modelled after Norway's sovereign wealth fund, holds billions of dollars from oil and gas revenues in the Timor Sea.

Togo.fact: The Koutammakou landscape, home to the Batammariba people, features remarkable tower-houses (Takienta) made of mud that serve as both dwellings and granaries.
The Akodessewa Fetish Market in Lomé is the world's largest voodoo market, selling animal skulls, herbs, and fetish objects used in West African spiritual practices.
The country is one of the narrowest in Africa, stretching just 50–100 km wide while extending over 500 km from coast to savanna.

Tonga.fact: It is the only remaining monarchy in the Pacific and one of the few countries in the world never formally colonised by a European power.
The Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai volcanic eruption in January 2022 was the most powerful explosion recorded in the 21st century, generating a tsunami and atmospheric shockwave felt around the world.
Rugby union is the de facto national sport, and per capita the country has produced more professional rugby players than any other nation.

Trinidad and Tobago.fact: Pitch Lake in southwest Trinidad is the world's largest natural deposit of asphalt, covering 40 hectares and estimated to contain 10 million tonnes of pitch.
The steelpan drum, the only acoustic musical instrument invented in the 20th century, was created here in the 1930s from discarded oil drums.
The country's Carnival is one of the largest in the world and features soca and calypso music that have influenced carnival celebrations globally.
It has one of the highest GDPs per capita in the Caribbean, largely due to its oil and natural gas industry.

Tunisia.fact: The Amphitheatre of El Jem, built around 238 AD, is one of the largest and best-preserved Roman amphitheatres in the world, rivalling the Colosseum in Rome.
The ancient city of Carthage, founded in the 9th century BC and famously destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, lies within the suburbs of modern-day Tunis.
Multiple Star Wars films used locations in the Saharan south — the town of Tataouine lent its name to Luke Skywalker's home planet Tatooine.
The country sparked the Arab Spring in December 2010 and is often cited as the only country where the movement resulted in a lasting democratic transition.

Turkey.fact: Göbekli Tepe, dating to approximately 9500 BC, is the world's oldest known temple complex — predating Stonehenge by about 6,000 years.
Cappadocia's fairy chimneys (tall, cone-shaped rock formations) were hollowed out to create underground cities that once sheltered up to 20,000 people.
The Grand Bazaar in Istanbul, with over 4,000 shops across 61 covered streets, is one of the oldest and largest covered markets in the world, dating to 1461.
Tulips were first cultivated here, not in the Netherlands — the Dutch imported the bulbs from the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century.
The city of Istanbul is the only metropolis in the world situated on two continents: Europe and Asia

Turkmenistan.fact: The Darvaza gas crater ('Door to Hell') has been burning continuously since 1971, when Soviet engineers set fire to a collapsed drilling rig to prevent methane spread — they expected it to burn out in weeks.
The former president Saparmurat Niyazov renamed the months of the year after himself and his family, banned dogs from the capital, and installed a rotating gold statue of himself.
The Karakum Desert covers roughly 70% of the country and contains some of the world's largest natural gas reserves.
The Akhal-Teke horse breed, originating here, has a metallic golden sheen to its coat and is sometimes called the 'most beautiful horse in the world'.

Turks and Caicos Islands.fact: Grace Bay Beach on Providenciales is consistently ranked among the best beaches in the world, with powdery white sand and turquoise water.
The islands were once a major centre of sea salt production, and the historic salinas on Grand Turk are now home to flamingo colonies.
The territory has considered several proposals to join Canada over the years, most recently in 2004, though none have advanced.

Tuvalu.fact: With a maximum elevation of just 4.6 metres, it is the second-lowest-lying country in the world (after the Maldives) and faces existential threat from rising sea levels.
The .tv internet domain generates significant national revenue — the country licences it to media and streaming companies worldwide.
It is the fourth-smallest country in the world by area (26 sq km) and one of the least visited, receiving only about 2,000 tourists per year.

Uganda.fact: The source of the White Nile flows out of Lake Victoria at Jinja, marking the beginning of the world's longest river's journey to the Mediterranean.
Bwindi Impenetrable Forest is home to roughly half of the world's remaining mountain gorillas.
The country straddles the equator and contains parts of both Lake Victoria (Africa's largest lake) and the Albertine Rift, one of the most biodiverse regions in Africa.
Winston Churchill called it 'the Pearl of Africa' after visiting in 1907, impressed by its natural beauty, climate, and wildlife.
It has been ranked as the most entrepreneurial country in the world, with roughly 28% of the population starting their own businesses.

Ukraine.fact: The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, site of the 1986 nuclear disaster, has become an accidental nature reserve where wolves, wild horses, and other wildlife now thrive.
The Tunnel of Love near Klevan is a 3-km railway passage through an arched canopy of trees, creating one of the world's most romantic-looking tunnels.
The country is home to some of the most fertile soil on Earth — its chernozem (black soil) covers roughly a third of the world's total supply.
The pysanka tradition of decorating eggs with intricate wax-resist designs dates back thousands of years and is recognised as an important cultural heritage.
The world’s deepest subway station, Arsenalna, is located in Kyiv at 105.5 meters (346 feet) underground.

United Arab Emirates.fact: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai stands at 828 metres — so tall that residents on the top floors see the sun set several minutes later than people at ground level.
The Palm Jumeirah, an artificial archipelago shaped like a palm tree, added 78 km of shoreline to Dubai's coast.
Abu Dhabi's Louvre museum is built over the sea with a dome of 7,850 metal stars creating a 'rain of light' effect inspired by the pattern of overlapping palm fronds.
The country went from a collection of fishing and pearling villages to one of the world's wealthiest nations in just 50 years after oil was discovered in the 1960s.
The police force in Dubai includes a fleet of supercars, including Lamborghinis, Ferraris, and Aston Martins, used primarily for patrolling tourist areas.

United Kingdom.fact: The Royal Mail has been delivering letters since 1516, making it one of the oldest postal services in the world.
The London Underground, opened in 1863, was the world's first underground railway — today it carries nearly 5 million passengers per day.
The Greenwich Meridian (0° longitude) passes through the Royal Observatory in London, establishing the basis for global time zones since 1884.
The country has over 1,500 listed stone circles, and the tradition of afternoon tea only dates to the 1840s, when the Duchess of Bedford invented it to bridge the gap between lunch and dinner.
For its size, Britain has more tornadoes than any other country in the world.

United States.fact: The Library of Congress contains over 170 million items, making it the largest library in the world by catalogue size.
Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano whose magma chamber could fill the Grand Canyon over 11 times — its last full eruption was 640,000 years ago.
The interstate highway system was partly inspired by President Eisenhower's experience with the German Autobahn and was originally justified as a military defence project.
Hawaii's Mauna Kea, measured from its base on the ocean floor, rises over 10,000 metres — taller than Mount Everest measured from sea level.
The phrase "keep the ball rolling" comes from the 1840 presidential campaign, where supporters literally rolled a 10-foot tin and leather ball from town to town.

United States Virgin Islands.fact: The territory was purchased from Denmark in 1917 for $25 million in gold — the only US territory acquired by purchase from a European power.
Trunk Bay on St John, surrounded by the Virgin Islands National Park, is regularly voted one of the world's most beautiful beaches.
Traffic drives on the left side of the road, a holdover from the Danish colonial era, despite using American left-hand-drive vehicles.

Uruguay.fact: The country hosted and won the first ever FIFA World Cup in 1930, and its team has won two World Cups despite a population of only about 3.5 million.
In 2013, it became the first country in the world to fully legalise the production, sale, and consumption of recreational cannabis.
Nearly 98% of the country's electricity comes from renewable sources, primarily hydroelectric and wind power.
Uruguayans consume more beef per capita than almost any other country — about 50 kg per person per year.
It was the first country in the world to fully legalize the production, sale, and consumption of cannabis in 2013.

Uzbekistan.fact: Samarkand's Registan Square, flanked by three madrasas covered in brilliant blue tilework, is considered one of the most stunning public squares in the world.
Along with Liechtenstein, it is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world — both the country and all its neighbours are landlocked.
The mathematician and astronomer al-Khwarizmi, born near Khiva around 780 AD, wrote the foundational text on algebra — the word 'algorithm' derives from his name.
The country is one of the world's largest cotton producers, though the industry has been criticised for historical use of forced labour during harvest season.

Vanuatu.fact: Land diving on Pentecost Island, where men jump from tall wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, is the original inspiration for modern bungee jumping.
The country has the highest density of languages per capita in the world — over 100 indigenous languages for a population of roughly 300,000.
Mount Yasur on Tanna Island has been erupting continuously for over 800 years and is one of the most accessible active volcanoes in the world.
It was ranked the happiest country in the world by the Happy Planet Index despite being one of the poorest in the Pacific.
This Pacific nation is the birthplace of bungee jumping; locals have practiced "land diving" (Nagol) for centuries using vines tied to their ankles.

Vatican City.fact: The Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512, covers over 500 square metres and contains more than 300 figures.
The Vatican Secret Archives contain over 85 km of shelving and include documents dating back to the 8th century, including a letter from Mary Queen of Scots written before her execution.
It has its own post office, pharmacy, and radio station, but no permanent maternity ward — no one has been born there in modern times.

The Swiss Guard, who protect the Pope, have served continuously since 1506 and still wear uniforms designed in a Renaissance style, though the popular attribution to Michelangelo is likely apocryphal.
It is the only country in the world where the birth rate is zero (since there are no maternity hospitals and citizenship is granted by office, not birth).

Venezuela.fact: Catatumbo lightning occurs at the mouth of the Catatumbo River for up to 300 nights per year, producing an estimated 1.2 million lightning strikes annually.
The tepui (table-top mountains) of the Gran Sabana inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel 'The Lost World' — their flat summits are home to species found nowhere else on Earth.
The country sits atop the world's largest proven oil reserves, surpassing even Saudi Arabia.
Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas, led the liberation of six nations from Spanish rule and is one of the most revered figures in Latin American history.

Vietnam.fact: Hang Sơn Đoòng, discovered in 2009, is the world's largest cave by volume — so large that a 747 could fly through its biggest chamber.
The country is the world's second-largest coffee producer (after Brazil), specialising in robusta beans, and Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk is now globally popular.
Halong Bay contains roughly 1,600 limestone islands and islets, many of which are hollow with enormous caves, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Vietnamese writing system (chữ Quốc ngữ) uses the Latin alphabet with extensive diacritical marks — it was developed by Portuguese missionaries in the 17th century.
It is the world’s largest exporter of cashew nuts and the second-largest exporter of coffee.

Wallis and Futuna.fact: The territory has three traditional kingdoms (Uvea, Alo, and Sigave) that still function alongside the French administration, each with its own king.
With a population of roughly 11,000 and no tourism industry to speak of, it is one of the most isolated and least-visited inhabited places on Earth.
There are no hotels on Futuna island — visitors must arrange to stay with local families.

Western Sahara.fact: It is one of the most sparsely populated territories in the world and has been the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Morocco and the Sahrawi independence movement since 1975.
A 2,700-km sand wall (the Berm), lined with millions of landmines, divides the territory between Moroccan-controlled areas and a Polisario-held buffer zone.
The territory has some of the world's richest phosphate deposits and fishing grounds, which are central to the economic dimension of the sovereignty dispute.

Yemen.fact: The old walled city of Shibam in the Hadramaut Valley contains mud-brick tower houses up to 11 stories tall, built as early as the 16th century — it is called the 'Manhattan of the Desert'.
Socotra Island, 350 km south of the mainland, has such unique flora that a third of its plant species are found nowhere else — the dragon blood tree is its most iconic species.
Coffee drinking culture originated in the Yemeni port of Mocha in the 15th century, and the word 'mocha' still refers to a style of coffee.
The Queen of Sheba, mentioned in the Bible and Quran, is traditionally believed to have ruled from the ancient kingdom of Saba in present-day Yemen.
The city of Shibam is known as the "Manhattan of the Desert" because it contains 16th-century mud-brick high-rises that are up to 11 stories tall.

Zambia.fact: Victoria Falls, on the border with Zimbabwe, is the world's largest sheet of falling water at 1,708 metres wide and 108 metres tall — the spray can be seen from 50 km away.
The Bangweulu Wetlands are home to the shoebill stork, a prehistoric-looking bird with a shoe-shaped bill that can stand over 1.5 metres tall.
The country has one of the highest rates of urbanisation in sub-Saharan Africa, with roughly 45% of the population living in cities along the 'line of rail'.

In 1964, shortly before independence, Zambia's space programme — consisting of one man, a 17-year-old girl, a missionary, and a cat — made international headlines for its plan to beat the US and USSR to the Moon.
In the 1960s, a schoolteacher named Edward Makuka Nkoloso started a space program to beat the US and USSR to the moon using a catapult system.

Zimbabwe.fact: Great Zimbabwe, the medieval stone city that gives the country its name, was the largest stone structure in sub-Saharan Africa built before the modern era, covering over 700 hectares.
During hyperinflation in 2008, the country printed a 100-trillion-dollar banknote — at the time barely enough to buy a loaf of bread.
The balancing rocks at Epworth near Harare are so iconic that they appear on the country's banknotes.
Lake Kariba, created by the dam of the same name, is the world's largest artificial lake by volume and was a major engineering feat of the 1950s.
At one point during its hyperinflation crisis, the government issued a 100-trillion-dollar note, which was barely enough to buy a loaf of bread.
